rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydia psittaci, a bacterial infection that usually affects birds.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: The infection can pass from birds to humans and cause respiratory illness.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Birds may transmit infection even when they show no symptoms.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Human transmission occurs mainly by inhaling infected respiratory particles or dust contaminated by bird faeces or secretions.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Bird owners, bird fanciers, pet-shop employees, poultry workers, veterinarians and wildlife or zoo workers can be at increased risk.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: The typical incubation period is between one and four weeks.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: PCR testing of respiratory samples is the preferred method for confirming human infection, with UKHSA reference-laboratory support available.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Prevention includes reducing accumulation of droppings, feathers and secretions and maintaining good ventilation where birds congregate.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: Psittacosis risk depends on bird species, infection status, dust generation, ventilation, exposure intensity, occupation, host factors and treatment timing.

rows.source: UKHSA psittacosis prevention and diagnosis
rows.verified: UKHSA psittacosis evidence is bird-, environment-, exposure-, person-, laboratory- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory-infection probability.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: Hantaviruses are carried mainly by rodents such as rats, mice and voles.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: People can become infected through exposure to infected rodent urine, faeces or saliva.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: Exposure can occur by inhaling contaminated particles and may also occur through cuts, eyes or, rarely, rodent bites.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: Most hantaviruses do not spread between people, although Andes virus has demonstrated person-to-person transmission in rare circumstances.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: Illness ranges from mild flu-like disease to severe respiratory disease or haemorrhagic disease with kidney involvement.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: UKHSA's Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory is the designated UK diagnostic laboratory for hantavirus testing.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: There is no proven specific treatment for most hantavirus infections and treatment is supportive.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: People travelling or working in endemic areas should reduce contact with rodents and avoid disturbing contaminated dust.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: Hantavirus risk depends on virus strain, rodent species, endemic area, exposure route, dust disturbance, travel, host factors and care timing.

rows.source: UKHSA hantavirus prevention and clinical guidance
rows.verified: UKHSA hantavirus evidence is strain-, rodent-, exposure-, traveller-, patient- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
